# Sequence and Mid-Level Movement

Category `seq`.

**Part 1 of 2.** 33 cards across five sections: what a sequence is, building and joining sequences, sequence types, rhythm and placement, and diagnosis and repair.

The sequence is the level between the scene and the act: two to six scenes bound by one tension, one question and one climax. Most writers plan acts and write scenes, and skip everything in between. That gap is where second acts die — a run of individually competent scenes that adds up to nothing, because nothing was ever asked across them.

## Section 1 — What a Sequence Is

### What Holds the Run Together

**Also called:** the sequence selector, the run selector, binding before type
**What it is:** The card at the head of the `seq.` shelf. It does not describe a run. It asks the three questions the shelf's own pair graph asks over and over — **what holds these scenes together, whose decision is the run's length, and does the run take things away or hand them out** — and returns a named shortlist for each answer. The axes were read off the shelf's `Yields to:` conditions and its `Avoid when:` lines, and the conditions that repeated became the questions. Every card named here is named by id.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This card never reaches the page. It exists so that the run that does reach the page was chosen against the material, the format and the character's supplies, rather than reached for because it is the kind of run the writer last wrote.
**Used for and where it works best:** **Ask the gate question before axis one, out loud, in one sentence: is this material a run at all?** More conditions on this shelf turn on that than on anything else, and its wrong answer is expensive in both directions — material that is one unbroken event written as four scenes, or a movement of the story summarised in one. If the honest answer is *one scene*, *one line*, or *one paragraph*, the answer is not on this shelf, and the first row of the axis two table names the shelf that takes over. If the honest answer is *more than one question*, you are choosing an act, not a run, and `struct.` owns it. Only then ask the three axes, in order, one sentence each. The first eliminates roughly half the file; the second and third leave a shortlist of three to six. Where two answers to axis one fight for one run, that is two runs and the join between them is `seq.sequence_handoff`.
**Best in:** formats: all | genres: all
**Avoid when:** **Do not run it on a draft you have not finished.** Both of this shelf's diagnostic cards refuse that themselves — `seq.boundary_test` because mapping seams in growing material freezes decisions you have not earned, and `seq.sequence_map` because mapping an incomplete manuscript maps your intentions, which are always better structured than the thing you wrote. And **distrust axis one whenever your honest answer is its first value.** More than half the shelf lives under *one pursuit*, so on an ordinary goal-driven run this map has two questions left and is doing rather less than half the work it does on an ensemble, a ceremony or a crosscut. The deeper limit is what the map is made of: **the pair graph on this shelf is a graph of run types.** Readers writing these fields were comparing one kind of run with another kind of run, so the map sorts types well, sorts bindings adequately, and does not sort a join from a join or a planning document from a planning document at all. If your answer to axis one is its fourth value, the map has handed you the whole planning and joinery region in one undivided block, and you are choosing inside it unaided.
**Example:**
> Material: a woman gets her brother out of a police station overnight, across four scenes.
> **Gate —** is it a run? Four scenes, one pressing question, one climax. Yes.
> **Axis one —** what holds it together? One pursuit. Not the station; she would follow him anywhere.
> **Axis two —** whose decision is the length? Hers, and mine. A feature, not a broadcast act.
> **Axis three —** subtract or accumulate? Subtract: each hour costs a favour she cannot ask twice.
> Shortlist, the intersection: `seq.sequence_spine`, `seq.internal_escalation`, `seq.decision_run`, `seq.negotiation_sequence`, `seq.journey_sequence`.
> Chosen: spine plus escalation on the axis of exposure, closed with `seq.partial_resolution`. The coat he walks out in is the residue.

---

**The axes**

**Axis 1 — What holds these scenes together: a pursuit, a container, or two things read against each other?**
Asked first because it is the condition the shelf repeats most on-shelf: fourteen `Yields to:` lines turn on it, and they are stated as facts about the material rather than as effects — *"Polyphonic run no single want organises"* (`seq.sequence_spine`), its exact reverse *"One character clearly drives the run"* (`seq.unifying_frame`), *"Mosaic where absence of causation is the point"* (`seq.scene_welding`), *"Only one thread is interesting"* (`seq.crosscut_sequence`), *"Threads have nothing to say to each other"* (`seq.convergence_sequence`), *"Engine is movement or discovery, not containment"* (`seq.siege_sequence`), *"Run deliberately aimless; hold pressure, ask nothing"* (`seq.sequence_question`), *"The second thread exists only to relieve pace"* (`seq.subplot_interleave`). Two cards on neighbouring shelves reach in on the same question — `beat.` sends a reader to `seq.ritual_sequence` when the evenness is the point, and `struct.` sends one to `seq.chapter_cluster` when linkage is too tight for stories to stand alone.

**Axis 2 — Is the run's length yours to choose, or has something already chosen it?**
The largest condition on the shelf once its off-shelf edges are counted: twenty-one lines turn on scale and format together, and its first answer leaves the shelf altogether — *"One unbroken event, one place, one pressure"* (`seq.sequence_unit`), *"Destination matters and the travel does not"* (`seq.journey_sequence`), *"The choice fits one scene, not a run"* (`seq.decision_run`), *"A single scene, not a complete run"* (`seq.cold_open_sequence`), *"One scene, or the rite broken from outside"* (`seq.ritual_sequence`), *"The past is information, not an event"* (`seq.embedded_past_run`). The rest of it names the owner of the clock: *"Rigid broadcast slots with fixed act lengths"* (`seq.length_variation`), *"Older children; a second thread is expected"* (`seq.kids_run`), *"Adapting long-form instead of restructuring it"* (`seq.shortform_serial`), *"Short form with no room for three placements"* (`seq.comic_run`).

**Axis 3 — Does the run take things away, or hand things out?**
Six conditions turn on it and it is asked last because it is the only axis that separates the type block from the inside, where the first two leave it whole: *"The coming run must be improvised"* (`seq.preparation_sequence`), *"No preparation, no resources, cover already blown"* (`seq.infiltration_sequence`), its exact reverse *"The weak point is already known; it is a heist"* (`seq.escape_sequence`), *"Character armed, competent and expecting trouble"* (`seq.stalk_sequence`), *"Lateral run: knowledge changes, cost does not"* (`seq.internal_escalation`), and a neighbouring shelf reaching in on the same test — `sig.` sends a reader to `seq.escape_sequence` when there is no escalation at every step. The shelf states the axis in its own words where it is strongest: a siege escalates by subtraction and not by attack, a journey removes a resource at every stage, an escape strips one capability per scene, an infiltration escalates on scrutiny while the debts pile up behind it.

**The default, and the one against it**

**The default is `seq.sequence_spine` holding the run and `seq.partial_resolution` closing it — and it is measured, not asserted.** `seq.sequence_spine` is the shelf's true default by the count that matters: three cards send a reader to it, and the three fire on **three different conditions from three different regions** — `seq.unifying_frame` (*"One character clearly drives the run"*), `seq.crosscut_sequence` (*"Only one thread is interesting"*) and `seq.mid_run_turn` (*"Short run, or a single unswerving pursuit"*). A container run, a two-strand run and a mid-run repair all fall back to the same place, which is what a fallback is. `seq.partial_resolution` is the close because it names its own universality — use it at the end of every internal run and nowhere else — and because the new question must be produced by the win rather than bolted onto it, which is the difference between a run that will not let a reader stop and a phone ringing for no reason.

**And the most-yielded-to card on this shelf is not the default.** `seq.breather_sequence` takes five inbound edges, more than anything else here, and **all five fire on one condition: the pressure has to come down.** `seq.partial_resolution` sends a reader there for a resting point after a long climb, `seq.spanning_tension` when the run's job is relief, `seq.subplot_interleave` when the second thread exists only to relieve pace, and two `beat.` cards from the neighbouring shelf for a becalmed stretch and for a scene that is a plateau by design. Five edges, one reason. It is the shelf's pressure-relief valve, not what the shelf falls back on.

**The one against it is `seq.thematic_run`.** Nothing routes to it; it is named by no `Yields to:` anywhere in the package; and it is the only card on this shelf where **the unit stops being one run**. Every other card here is built to make a single run work. This one needs two, deliberately shaped alike, given to different people, and the story's claim is the difference between what the same want costs each of them — a caution on a record against a job, a flat and a child's school place. Nobody says the claim, and the reader does the arithmetic. Its cost is stated plainly in its own `Avoid when:` and it is not small: built on a claim you have not decided, it rigs itself. **Its near cousin against the grain is `seq.imagined_sequence`** — the only run here whose material never happened, the only one that prices itself as a withdrawal from a finite account, and likewise never yielded to by anything.

---

**The unasked**

**Twenty-six of the fifty-one reachable cards are the target of no `Yields to:` field anywhere in the package.** They can be chosen and nothing ever sends you to them. By id:

`seq.sequence_question` · `seq.scene_welding` · `seq.dangling_cause` · `seq.internal_escalation` · `seq.sequence_handoff` · `seq.preparation_sequence` · `seq.montage_sequence` · `seq.convergence_sequence` · `seq.act_rhythm` · `seq.shortform_serial` · `seq.mid_run_turn` · `seq.run_entry_context` · `seq.count_vs_runtime` · `seq.subplot_interleave` · `seq.thematic_run` · `seq.decision_run` · `seq.cold_open_sequence` · `seq.embedded_past_run` · `seq.imagined_sequence` · `seq.hearing_sequence` · `seq.negotiation_sequence` · `seq.siege_sequence` · `seq.comic_run` · `seq.kids_run` · `seq.player_paced_run` · `seq.documentary_sequence`

**And the shape of that list is the finding, not its length.** Every card that joins, enters, orders or paces a run is on it — `seq.scene_welding`, `seq.dangling_cause`, `seq.internal_escalation`, `seq.sequence_handoff`, `seq.mid_run_turn`, `seq.run_entry_context`, `seq.act_rhythm`. **The whole joinery region yields outward and nothing yields inward.** The pair graph on this shelf is a graph of *types*: a reader writing one of these fields was holding one kind of run and comparing it with another kind of run, and a seam is not an alternative to a seam. `seq.sequence_handoff` says so in its own words — *every sequence has a handoff whether you design it or not, and the only real error is not choosing one* — which is precisely a card that cannot be the second half of a pair, because there is nothing to prefer it to.

The second thing the list shows: **every run that lives inside another run is unasked** — `seq.cold_open_sequence`, `seq.embedded_past_run`, `seq.imagined_sequence`, and with them the medium cards `seq.kids_run`, `seq.player_paced_run` and `seq.documentary_sequence`. A nested run has no alternative of the form *in situation X, that card instead*, because its alternative is **not nesting at all**, and that alternative lives on `time.`, `scene.` and `open.`. The pair field can only point sideways within a shelf or once across it; it cannot say *do not do this here, do it somewhere else in the structure*.

The third thing, and it is the card this shelf wants: **there is no card for a run that stops and restarts.** The shelf has a clean join, two runs cut together, and a run dropped whole inside another — and nothing at all for a run that breaks off mid-question, lets twenty minutes of other material pass, and picks the same question up again, which is how most television and every long novel actually carries a thread. The nearest thing that exists records the gap in its own `Avoid when:` without anything routing a reader there to read it: `seq.mid_run_turn` says that a turn which changes the question means the run ended there and a new one began — and then hands the problem to `seq.boundary_test`, which will tell you where the seam is and nothing about how to sew the two halves back together across the gap.

**And five cards are reachable only from a failure.** `seq.sequence_unit`, `seq.sequence_climax`, `seq.partial_resolution`, `seq.boundary_test` and `seq.payoff_ledger` have exactly one inbound edge each, and in every case the source is a named failure and the edge is a repair instruction, not a route. The definition of a run, the rule for its biggest beat, the rule for how it closes, the test for where it starts and the ledger that keeps its promises — **this shelf points a reader at its own foundations only after they have got something wrong.**

`seq.what_holds_the_run`

### The Sequence Unit

**Also called:** mini-movie, movement, story block, act-within-an-act
**What it is:** A run of two to six scenes held together by a single pressing question, ending in a climax bigger than any climax inside it. It is the smallest unit of story that can be summarised as an event rather than as a conversation.
**Effect on the audience:** They stop tracking individual scenes and start tracking a situation. Attention shifts from "what is being said" to "how does this end", which is the state you want a reader in for most of a book or a film.
**Used for and where it works best:** Reach for the sequence unit whenever you are writing more than three scenes in a row inside one story thread. The craft rule: name the unit before you write it, in one line, as a verb the protagonist is doing — "gets the passport", "hides the body", "loses the witness". If you cannot write that line, you do not have a sequence, you have scenes in a row. See `struct.sequence_approach` for how these units tile a whole feature.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, audio drama | genres: thriller, crime, adventure, literary fiction
**Avoid when:** The material is genuinely one unbroken event in one place under one pressure — a dinner, an interrogation, a deathbed. Splitting that into three scenes to make it a "sequence" gets you three weak scenes instead of one strong one.
**Example:**
> Sequence: "Gets into the building."
> 1. She scouts the loading dock, times the guard, and is moved on by a cleaner who now knows her face.
> 2. She buys a courier jacket from a man who wants paying twice.
> 3. The delivery goes in — but the cleaner is on the desk, and looks up.
> 4. She talks past him badly; he waves her through and reaches for the phone.
> Four scenes, one question, one climax, and the climax costs her more than the win is worth.

**Yields to:** `time.real_time` — One unbroken event, one place, one pressure.  
`seq.sequence_unit`

---

### The Sequence Question

**Also called:** sub-goal question, mid-level dramatic question, the run's hook
**What it is:** The specific yes-or-no the sequence exists to answer, sitting above the scene questions and below the act question. It has a deadline, an owner and a visible outcome.
**Effect on the audience:** It gives them something to carry across a scene change. Without it every cut is a small reset; with it every cut is a step.
**Used for and where it works best:** Write it before anything else in the sequence. The craft rule: the sequence question must be answerable by an action the reader can see, not by a feeling. "Will he get the tape back before Friday?" is a sequence question. "Will he heal?" is a theme. Nest it properly — the scene question in `scene.scene_question` is a step toward it, never a restatement of it.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, serialised fiction | genres: thriller, mystery, heist, courtroom, romance
**Avoid when:** The run is deliberately aimless — a drift, a bereavement, a stretch where the point is that nothing can be done. Imposing a question there falsifies the experience and reads as a writer panicking about pace.
**Example:**
> Weak: a run of scenes in which a detective "investigates the fire".
> Sharpened: "Can she get the insurance file before the adjuster's office closes at five and shreds it?"
> The same three scenes — the phone call, the drive, the argument at the desk — but now the clock is inside every one of them, and the reader is watching a hand move.

**Yields to:** `seq.spanning_tension` — Run deliberately aimless; hold pressure, ask nothing.  
`seq.sequence_question`

---

### The Sequence Spine

**Also called:** the through-line of the run, the sequence want
**What it is:** The one continuous pursuit running underneath every scene in the sequence, so each scene is another attempt at the same thing rather than a new thing.
**Effect on the audience:** Cohesion. They feel the scenes as one gesture, the way you feel a paragraph rather than a list of sentences.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it as the test when a sequence feels busy but inert. The craft rule: write the same sentence at the top of every scene in the run — "she is trying to get the passport" — and if it is a lie for any scene, that scene belongs to a different sequence or to nowhere. This is the sequence-level version of what `struct.mckee_sequence` describes above it.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, stage play | genres: heist, adventure, procedural, thriller
**Avoid when:** You are writing a deliberately fragmented or polyphonic passage where the point is that no single want organises the people in it. A war-novel chapter cluster covering six unconnected soldiers has no spine and should not be given a fake one.
**Example:**
> Spine: "He is trying to get his daughter to speak to him."
> 1. He waits outside her school; she walks past him to the bus.
> 2. He calls; the boyfriend answers and is polite, which is worse.
> 3. He turns up at her work with the money; she takes it and says thank you, sir.
> 4. He follows her home, and she finally turns around and speaks — and it ends him.
> Every scene is the same attempt. That is the only reason the fourth one lands.

**Yields to:** `seq.unifying_frame` — Polyphonic run no single want organises.  
`seq.sequence_spine`

---

### The Sequence Climax

**Also called:** the run's payoff, the sequence turn, the big one
**What it is:** The last scene of the sequence, which answers the sequence question and turns a value harder than any scene before it in the run.
**Effect on the audience:** Release plus forward pressure. They get an answer and a new problem in the same beat, which is why they keep going.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it whenever you have built four scenes and need to know which one is last. The craft rule: the climax scene's value turn must outweigh the sum of the turns before it — if scene three is the biggest thing that happens, scene three is your climax and scenes four and five are epilogue, so cut them or move them. Measure the turn with `scene.value_turn` and price the run with `scene.escalating_cost`.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, audio drama | genres: thriller, crime, war, romance, horror
**Avoid when:** The sequence deliberately ends in anticlimax as a statement — the raid that finds an empty house. That still has to be the biggest beat in the run emotionally, or it is not a decision, it is a shortfall.
**Example:**
> Run of four: argues with the lawyer (hope to doubt) → finds the second signature (doubt to alarm) → confronts his brother, who denies it (alarm to certainty) → burns the document.
> The burn is the climax, and it has to destroy the only thing that would have cleared him. If the confrontation is the bigger beat, end on the confrontation and let the burn open the next sequence.

`seq.sequence_climax`

---

### Sequence as Short Film

**Also called:** the mini-movie model, the short-film analogy, sequence three-act
**What it is:** Treating each sequence as a complete small story with its own setup, complication and climax, so the ten to fifteen minutes would stand up if you pulled them out.
**Effect on the audience:** Every stretch feels shaped and finished, even mid-act, so the middle never feels like waiting.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when a second act is beating you — writing eight fifteen-minute films is tractable in a way that writing seventy pages of "middle" is not. The craft rule that separates this from a gimmick: the short film must resolve only partially. A sequence that closes completely stops the film dead; see `seq.partial_resolution`.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, limited series, novella | genres: all narrative
**Avoid when:** The engine is accumulation rather than episode — a slow marriage collapse, a grief novel. Cutting those into eight self-contained films gives you eight neat units and no accumulation.
**Example:**
> Sequence as short film — "The Audition":
> Setup: she lies about her age to get the slot. Complication: the accompanist is the man she lied to last year. Climax: she sings, he plays it wrong on purpose, she finishes anyway, she gets the job.
> Standing alone it is a complete fifteen-minute short. Inside the feature it also plants the accompanist, who is the antagonist of the sequence after next.

**Yields to:** `seq.chapter_cluster` — Engine is accumulation, not self-contained episodes.  
`seq.short_film_model`

---

### Partial Resolution

**Also called:** incomplete close, the open door, resolution with a residue
**What it is:** Answering the sequence question while opening a larger one, so the run ends satisfied but not finished.
**Effect on the audience:** The specific sensation of not being able to stop — the question they came in with is answered, and a bigger one arrived while they were watching.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it at the end of an internal sequence, apart from the cases under Avoid when, and nowhere else. The craft rule: the new question must be produced by the win, not bolted onto it. The passport arrives and the name on it is wrong; the confession is recorded and the recorder was running the whole time. A bolted-on cliffhanger — a phone rings, unexplained — buys one page of attention and costs you trust for fifty.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, serialised novel, web serial | genres: thriller, mystery, horror, adventure
**Avoid when:** The sequence is the last one in the story, or it is a deliberate resting point after a long climb, or it is the single run of a young children's episode, which must close completely (`seq.kids_run`), with recurrence coming from the series format rather than an open danger. Two open doors in a row with no floor between them tires a reader faster than a lull does.
**Example:**
> Question: will she get her brother out of the station before charges are filed?
> Answer: yes — the desk sergeant releases him at 4 a.m.
> Residue: he walks out wearing someone else's coat, and does not explain it.
> The run is closed. The film is not.

**Yields to:** `seq.breather_sequence` — Deliberate resting point after a long climb.  
`seq.partial_resolution`

---

### Finding the Boundaries

**Also called:** the seam test, sequence demarcation, where one run ends
**What it is:** A diagnostic for locating where a sequence actually starts and stops in existing material, instead of guessing from page count.
**Effect on the audience:** None directly — this is a writer's tool. Its effect shows up as a draft that stops sprawling.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it on a finished draft, or on an outline that has gone shapeless. The craft rule, three tests in order: (1) the question test — where is a new question asked, and where is it answered; (2) the pressure test — where does tension sit at its lowest, because that is a seam; (3) the summary test — can you name the block with one active verb phrase. Boundaries usually sit one scene earlier than writers think, because the first scene of the new run gets mistaken for the coda of the old one.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama | genres: all
**Avoid when:** You are in a first draft you have not finished. Mapping seams in material that is still growing freezes decisions you have not earned.
**Example:**
> Pages 44 to 61, marked by the writer as one sequence. Applying the tests:
> p44–50 asks "will he find the address?" and answers it on p50.
> p51 is a quiet scene of him sitting in the car — the lowest pressure in the run, and the writer thought it was the end of the block.
> p51 is actually the opening of the next sequence: "will he go in?"
> Two sequences, not one, and the sagging middle was a seam, not a flaw.

`seq.boundary_test`

## Section 2 — Building and Joining

### Welding Scenes into a Sequence

**Also called:** scene chaining, causal welding, the because-therefore link
**What it is:** Making each scene the direct cause of the next, so the run reads as one event rather than a list.
**Effect on the audience:** Momentum. Cuts feel like consequences instead of the writer changing the subject.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it whenever the connective tissue between scenes is "and then" or "meanwhile". The craft rule: the last action of scene N must create the problem that opens scene N+1. If you can reorder two scenes in a run without breaking anything, they are not welded, they are stacked — and one of them should probably fuse into the other (`scene.merge_two_scenes`) or go.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, comics | genres: thriller, crime, heist, action, mystery
**Avoid when:** Writing a mosaic or a deliberately arbitrary passage — a plague year, a city at dawn — where the absence of causation is the point. Also avoid over-welding romance, where some scenes should feel like weather rather than consequence.
**Example:**
> Stacked: He searches the office. He meets the widow. He drives to the coast.
> Welded: He searches the office and takes the address book, which is missed → the widow calls him in to ask why he has it → he lies badly, so she gives him the coast address to get rid of him, wrong on purpose.
> The same three scenes. Now nothing can be moved.

**Yields to:** `seq.unifying_frame` — Mosaic where absence of causation is the point.  
`seq.scene_welding`

---

### The Dangling Cause

**Also called:** the planted intention, the forward hook, dialogue hook
**What it is:** A stated intention, warning, threat or prediction whose effect is deliberately delayed, so it hangs over the scenes between statement and payoff.
**Effect on the audience:** Low-grade continuous anticipation across a whole run. They carry the line into scenes that have nothing to do with it.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it at the head of a sequence to bind scenes that are otherwise loosely related, and on the out-line of a scene to pull across a cut. The craft rule: the dangle must be specific enough to be recognised when it lands. "Something bad will happen" dangles nothing; "If that van is still here on Sunday I'm burning it" dangles a Sunday. Pay it inside the same sequence or the next one — a dangle carried across three sequences reads as a forgotten thread, not as patience. That is tighter than the distance `seq.payoff_ledger` allows a plain plant, because a dangle works by hanging over the scenes between; one that must travel further is restated once in the middle, as the ledger says.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, audio drama | genres: thriller, crime, horror, family drama, comedy
**Avoid when:** The story depends on ambush rather than dread. Every dangle you plant converts a surprise into a countdown, and some scenes need the reader unprepared.
**Example:**
> Scene 1, out-line: "My father comes home Thursday. Don't be here Thursday."
> Scene 2: an unrelated job interview — but the reader is counting days.
> Scene 3: she buys a bed, delivery Friday, and the reader winces at the date.
> Scene 4: Thursday.

**Yields to:** `tens.earned_surprise` — Story depends on ambush, not countdown.  
`seq.dangling_cause`

---

### Spanning Tension

**Also called:** the tension that outlives the scene, sustained mid-level pressure
**What it is:** A pressure set up early in a sequence that stays unresolved through every scene in it — a deadline, a hunt, an unexploded fact — so that scenes with different content still share a temperature.
**Effect on the audience:** Scenes that are calm on the surface read as tense, because the reader supplies the pressure the writer established.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it to buy quiet scenes in the middle of a fast run. The craft rule: reassert the spanning tension at least once per scene, in one line or one image, or it decays — a glance at a clock, a mention of the flight, the dog still barking next door. Pair it with `tens.shrinking_options` when the pressure should also be narrowing the character's choices.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, stage play | genres: thriller, war, horror, domestic drama
**Avoid when:** The sequence's job is relief. If you have just paid off a set piece and the reader needs air, spanning tension denies them the trough that makes the next peak legible.
**Example:**
> Spanning tension: the body is in the boot of the car outside.
> 1. Lunch with the in-laws. Nobody mentions the car. The reader cannot see anything else.
> 2. The nephew asks to be driven to football. Refused, badly.
> 3. It starts to rain and the father-in-law offers to put the shopping "in your boot".
> The scenes are a lunch, a favour and a shopping trip. The sequence is a horror film.

**Yields to:** `seq.breather_sequence` — The run's job is relief.  
`seq.spanning_tension`

---

### The Unifying Frame

**Also called:** unity of place, unity of event, the container
**What it is:** Binding a run of scenes not by goal but by a shared container — one night, one building, one wedding, one crossing — so the frame itself supplies the cohesion.
**Effect on the audience:** They read the run as an occasion. Entrances and exits acquire weight, because inside a frame leaving means something.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when the material is genuinely multi-threaded and no single goal covers it — an ensemble, a party, a siege. The craft rule: a frame substitutes for a spine, never for a question. Something must still be at stake by the end of the night, or you have written an atmosphere. Compare `seq.sequence_spine`, which is the goal-based alternative.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, stage play | genres: ensemble, literary fiction, disaster, war, social drama
**Avoid when:** One character clearly drives the run. Framing by place then dilutes a perfectly good pursuit into a tour of rooms.
**Example:**
> Frame: the wedding, 4 p.m. to midnight.
> 1. The best man loses the rings in the car park.
> 2. The bride's mother recognises the caterer.
> 3. Speeches; the groom says the wrong name.
> 4. Midnight, the car park again, and the rings are in someone else's pocket.
> No single goal. One night, and nobody leaves it unchanged.

**Yields to:** `seq.sequence_spine` — One character clearly drives the run.  
`seq.unifying_frame`

---

### Internal Escalation

**Also called:** the rising run, sequence gradient, step-up structure
**What it is:** Ordering the scenes inside a sequence so each one costs more, risks more, or narrows the options further than the last.
**Effect on the audience:** They feel the floor tilting. Even without new information, later scenes read as more dangerous purely because of position.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it on any run of three or more scenes toward one goal. The craft rule: escalate one axis at a time and name it — cost, exposure, proximity, or irreversibility. Raising all four in every scene burns the run out by scene two. Build the rungs with `anta.obstacle_ladder` and price each one with `scene.escalating_cost`.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, game narrative | genres: thriller, heist, horror, action, crime
**Avoid when:** The sequence's interest is lateral rather than vertical — three interviews that change what we know without changing what it costs. Forcing escalation there produces melodrama in a story built on curiosity.
**Example:**
> Axis: exposure.
> 1. He asks a stranger about the address. Nobody who matters sees him.
> 2. He asks the porter, who writes his name in a book.
> 3. He asks the tenant, who telephones someone the moment he leaves.
> 4. He asks the man himself.
> The question never changes. His visibility triples every scene.

**Yields to:** `seq.investigation_sequence` — Lateral run: knowledge changes, cost does not.  
`seq.internal_escalation`

---

### The Sequence Handoff

**Also called:** sequence transition, the join, the seam beat
**What it is:** The deliberate craft of the moment between two sequences — how the old run's residue becomes the new run's problem.
**Effect on the audience:** Either a clean breath and a new grip, or a lurch. There is no neutral seam; readers feel joins even when they cannot name them.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it every time you close a sequence. The craft rule: pick one of three joins on purpose. **Hard cut** — end on the climax, open the next run mid-action, no bridge; fast, disorienting, right for thrillers. **Overlap** — the last scene of the old run is the first scene of the new one, doing double duty; elegant, hardest to write. **Trough** — one short quiet scene between runs so the cost can register; essential after a set piece. A seam you do not design defaults to a trough, and three unearned troughs is exactly what a slack second act is made of.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, serialised fiction | genres: all
**Avoid when:** Never — every sequence has a handoff whether you design it or not. The only real error is not choosing one.
**Example:**
> Overlap join. The last scene of the escape sequence is the car reaching the border town. The first scene of the hiding sequence is that same scene, forty seconds later, when she reads the hotel register and sees her husband's handwriting.
> One scene. Two runs. The join is invisible and the reader's grip never loosens.

`seq.sequence_handoff`

---

## Section 3 — Sequence Types

### The Action Sequence

**Also called:** the chase, the fight run, the physical set-to
**What it is:** A sequence whose scenes are physical attempts at one goal under time pressure, usually structured as a chain of plans that fail in escalating ways.
**Effect on the audience:** Sustained physiological arousal, but only if they can follow the geography and can name what would count as winning.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when the story's conflict has become physical and staying verbal would be a dodge. The craft rule that separates good action from noise: give the sequence beats, not moves. Each beat is a plan, an obstacle and a cost — "he tries the stairs, they are blocked, he loses the bag". Three to five beats, each closing an exit, and a final beat where the thing he has been protecting is the price of escape. Geography must be established before speed; the audience cannot feel a near miss in a space they cannot picture.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, comics, game narrative, novel | genres: action, thriller, war, adventure, crime
**Avoid when:** The outcome is never in doubt and the hero is invulnerable in the reader's mind. Then the sequence is choreography, and choreography is the editor's job, not the writer's.
**Example:**
> Rooftop chase, four beats:
> 1. He takes the fire escape — it ends two floors short. He jumps, and drops the phone with the only copy.
> 2. He goes for the phone on the ledge below — the pursuer reaches the roof first and now has the high ground.
> 3. He crosses to the next building through a flat with a family in it — and is seen, so now there are witnesses who can place him.
> 4. He gets out through the lobby, clean — leaving the phone on the ledge, which is the whole reason he came.

**Yields to:** `tens.chase_turn` — Outcome never in doubt; change the question instead.  
`seq.action_sequence`

---

### The Set Piece

**Also called:** the big one, the trailer moment, the showcase sequence
**What it is:** An extended sequence built around a single memorable premise — the vault, the opera house, the flooding tunnel — where the location or conceit generates the obstacles rather than merely hosting them.
**Effect on the audience:** The thing they describe to someone else afterwards. A set piece is the unit of word of mouth.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use two or three across a feature, roughly every twenty to thirty minutes, and one per television episode at most. The craft rule: the premise must be unusable anywhere else. If the sequence could be moved to a car park without changing a beat, it is an action scene with an expensive backdrop, not a set piece. The second rule: the set piece must turn the story. A spectacle that leaves the plot where it found it is the most expensive filler there is.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, series, comics, game narrative | genres: action, heist, adventure, comedy, disaster
**Avoid when:** Budget, register or scale would make it ridiculous, and in intimate drama generally. A set piece in a chamber film reads as the writer losing their nerve.
**Example:**
> Premise: a theft during a funeral, with the coffin as the only container nobody will open.
> 1. The mourners arrive; he is the one who carries the coffin, so he cannot put it down.
> 2. The widow wants it open for a last look; he talks her out of it and earns her attention for the rest of the day.
> 3. The wrong hearse takes it — to the crematorium.
> 4. He stops the burn by confessing to something else entirely, which is worse and true.
> Nothing here survives being moved to a car park.

**Yields to:** `seq.ritual_sequence` — Intimate or chamber drama, or scale would be ridiculous.  
`seq.set_piece`

---

### The Investigation Sequence

**Also called:** the enquiry run, the interview chain, procedural block
**What it is:** A run of scenes in which the character gathers information, each source changing the shape of the question rather than simply adding facts.
**Effect on the audience:** Curiosity as the engine instead of fear. They lean in rather than brace.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it whenever knowledge, not force, is what the character lacks. The craft rule: every interview must cost something or change the question; an interview that only transfers information is a briefing, and briefings do not belong in sequences. Order the sources so each one makes the previous answer wrong, and meter what the reader learns with `info.staged_reveal` so the reveals land on the sequence climax rather than on scene two.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, audio drama | genres: mystery, crime, legal, journalism, espionage
**Avoid when:** The reader is already ahead of the detective. Watching someone assemble what we assembled forty pages ago is the single most common cause of a dead second act in crime fiction.
**Example:**
> Question: who signed the release form?
> 1. The clerk says the signature is the doctor's — and mentions the doctor left in March.
> 2. The doctor, found in a garden centre, says he signed nothing in March because he was in hospital.
> 3. The hospital has no record of him — but has a record of the patient he supposedly discharged.
> 4. The patient is the person asking the questions.
> Four scenes, and the question is a different question in each.

**Yields to:** `tens.bomb_under_table` — Reader already ahead of the detective.  
`seq.investigation_sequence`

---

### The Preparation Sequence

**Also called:** the gear-up, the plan run, assembling the team
**What it is:** A sequence in which characters acquire the people, tools, knowledge or access needed for a later sequence, and in doing so acquire the liabilities that will wreck it.
**Effect on the audience:** Anticipation with a specific shape. They now know what the coming set piece requires, so they can feel each element go wrong.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it immediately before a set piece, never more than once per act. The craft rule: never let preparation be only preparation. Each acquisition must plant a flaw — the driver drinks, the map is ten years old, the man who can open the safe wants to be paid in a way that cannot be hidden. Preparation without planted flaws is shopping, and shopping does not have a climax.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, game narrative | genres: heist, war, sports, adventure
**Avoid when:** The coming sequence is meant to be improvised or chaotic. Preparing carefully and then throwing the plan away can be done, but only once per story and only if the throwing-away is the point.
**Example:**
> Three scenes, three flaws:
> 1. She recruits the driver — who takes the job because he needs money by Tuesday, which is two days before the robbery.
> 2. She buys the uniforms — from a shop whose owner photographs every customer for insurance.
> 3. She walks the route at the right hour — and meets a neighbour, who is delighted to see her there and will remember it.
> The heist has not started and it is already three-quarters lost.

**Yields to:** `seq.escape_sequence` — The coming run must be improvised.  
`seq.preparation_sequence`

---

### The Journey Sequence

**Also called:** the road run, the crossing, transit structure
**What it is:** A sequence organised by movement from one place to another, where each stage of the journey supplies a different pressure and the arrival is the climax.
**Effect on the audience:** Measurable progress. Distance is the most legible form of story movement there is, which is why it papers over weak plotting — and why it is dangerous.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when the geography genuinely alters the problem: crossing a border changes the law, crossing a river changes who can follow. The craft rule: each stage must remove a resource. Fuel, allies, cover, time, cash, nerve. A journey sequence in which the characters arrive with what they set out with is a travelogue, no matter how good the scenery.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, game narrative | genres: western, adventure, war, fantasy, migration
**Avoid when:** The destination matters and the travel does not. Then compress the whole thing to a line and open on arrival — nine times out of ten that is the better film.
**Example:**
> Four stages, four subtractions:
> 1. The bus as far as the checkpoint — they lose the papers to a soldier who keeps them.
> 2. On foot to the farm — they lose the younger brother, who stays because the farmer's daughter offers him a bed.
> 3. The truck at night — they lose the money, paying triple for the space.
> 4. The border at dawn — she crosses with nothing, which is the only reason she is let through.

**Yields to:** `time.ellipsis` — Destination matters and the travel does not.  
`seq.journey_sequence`

---

### The Montage as a Sequence

**Also called:** compression run, the passage of time block, the training block
**What it is:** A sequence of very short fragments standing in for a long process, structured so the fragments themselves form a rising line rather than a list of moments.
**Effect on the audience:** Time collapses without the reader feeling cheated of the process — provided the fragments show change, not repetition.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when the process matters but its individual days do not — training, recovery, a courtship, a business being built. The craft rule: a montage is still a sequence, so it still needs a question and a climax. Three to seven fragments, each showing a different stage of the same skill or relationship, and the last fragment must be a real scene with dialogue and a turn — that scene is your climax and the fragments are its setup. A montage that ends on another fragment ends on nothing.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, music video, comics | genres: sports, romance, war, biography, comedy
**Avoid when:** The process is the story. If the reader came for how a thing is built, compressing the building into ninety seconds tells them they came to the wrong film.
**Example:**
> Question: can he make the weight?
> Fragments: the scales, too high, and he looks away. Running at night, alone. Running at night, with the trainer. Eating nothing at his sister's table while everyone watches.
> Climax scene: the weigh-in — he makes it by half a pound, and the trainer says nothing, which is when he understands he is being sold.

**Yields to:** `scene.single_action_scene` — The process itself is the subject.  
`seq.montage_sequence`

---

### The Crosscut Sequence

**Also called:** parallel sequence, intercut run, parallel editing
**What it is:** Two or more sequences told in alternating fragments, so the reader holds both at once and the cuts themselves create meaning.
**Effect on the audience:** Tension from what neither side knows, or irony from what only the reader knows. The cut becomes a rhetorical device rather than a transition.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when two threads are on a collision course, or when two simultaneous events comment on each other. The craft rules that actually matter: establish each thread properly before you begin cutting — if the fragments are short from the first beat, you have nowhere to accelerate to. Shorten the fragments as the sequence rises, and make the final cut land on the thread with the most to lose. Use one clock the reader can see, or the simultaneity is an assertion rather than an experience.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel, comics | genres: thriller, crime, war, horror, disaster
**Avoid when:** Only one thread is interesting. Crosscutting to a weak thread does not strengthen it; it teaches the reader to skim, and they will skim the strong thread too once the habit sets in.
**Example:**
> A: the christening, in the church.
> B: four murders across the city.
> Early: two long blocks, a full baptism, a full car journey.
> Middle: the priest's questions and the answers begin to alternate, half a page each.
> Late: one line per cut — the renunciation of Satan against a door opening.
> Final cut lands on A: he says "I do renounce them", and the sequence is over.

**Yields to:** `seq.sequence_spine` — Only one thread is interesting.  
`seq.crosscut_sequence`

---

### The Convergence Sequence

**Also called:** the gathering, the collision run, threads-meeting sequence
**What it is:** A sequence whose whole structure is separated characters or threads being drawn into the same place, with the meeting as the climax.
**Effect on the audience:** Mounting inevitability. Once they can see the shape, every scene is read as a step toward a collision they can already picture.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it at the end of an act, especially the second, and in ensemble stories where the threads have run separately for too long. The craft rule: the reader must see the convergence coming at least two scenes before the characters do — that gap is the entire pleasure. And the meeting must be worse than any single thread was: if two people who both want the same thing finally meet and simply talk, you built a corridor to an empty room.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, series | genres: crime, ensemble drama, disaster, thriller, epic fantasy
**Avoid when:** The threads have nothing to say to each other. Forced convergence — everyone happens to be at the same airport — is the most visible plotting there is.
**Example:**
> Three threads, one hotel, one night.
> 1. The debtor books the room under a false name; we see the name.
> 2. The collector takes a job that gives him a false name — the same one.
> 3. The wife, looking for neither, is given the room number by a clerk being helpful.
> 4. Three knocks on one door in four minutes. The reader has known for ten pages, which is why they cannot look away.

**Yields to:** `seq.crosscut_sequence` — Threads have nothing to say to each other.  
`seq.convergence_sequence`

---

## Section 4 — Rhythm and Placement

### Sequence Rhythm Across an Act

**Also called:** act-level pacing, the run-of-runs, sequence pattern
**What it is:** Designing the sequence of sequences inside one act so the act itself rises, rather than being four blocks of equal intensity laid end to end.
**Effect on the audience:** An act that feels like it is going somewhere even when no single scene is spectacular.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when an act reads as competent and exhausting at the same time. The craft rule: no two adjacent sequences should share a mode. If sequence one is an investigation, sequence two should be physical or intimate; if sequence three is a set piece, sequence four is short and quiet. Then check that the last sequence in the act contains the act's biggest turn — see `struct.mckee_act`. Four sequences at the same pitch reads slower than four sequences at descending pitch, because the reader has stopped measuring.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, hour drama, novel | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The act is deliberately monotonous as an effect — an imprisonment, an institutional grind. Even then, vary the length rather than the pitch.
**Example:**
> A second act that failed: chase, chase, argument, chase.
> The fix, same material: chase (physical) → the flat, unpacking what the chase cost (intimate, ten minutes) → the archive, learning who sent them (investigation) → the chase that ends in the river (physical, twice the length of the first).
> Nothing was added. The act now rises because no two runs are the same shape.

**Yields to:** `seq.length_variation` — Act deliberately monotonous; vary length, not pitch.  
`seq.act_rhythm`

---

### Varying Sequence Length

**Also called:** irregular runs, length as rhythm, the short sequence
**What it is:** Deliberately unequal sequences — a two-scene run against a six-scene run — so that duration itself carries meaning.
**Effect on the audience:** Subliminal pacing. A short run after a long one reads as a sharp intake of breath; a long one after several short ones reads as being trapped.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it as the first repair when a draft is technically correct and rhythmically dead. The craft rule: put your shortest sequence immediately after your longest, and immediately before your biggest. The eight-sequence model's tidy ten-to-fifteen-minute blocks are a planning convenience, not a delivery target — `struct.seq_d` and `struct.seq_f` in a good film are routinely very different lengths.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, serialised fiction | genres: thriller, horror, literary fiction, war
**Avoid when:** You are writing to a rigid slot structure with fixed act lengths — some broadcast and branded formats genuinely will not take it.
**Example:**
> Long run: the six-scene siege of the farmhouse, twenty minutes.
> Short run: two scenes, four minutes — burying the dog, and the drive out.
> Long run: the city, and everything that was decided over the dog's grave going wrong.
> The four-minute run is the one people remember, and it only works because of the twenty minutes on either side.

**Yields to:** `seq.tv_act_sequence` — Rigid broadcast slots with fixed act lengths.  
`seq.length_variation`

---

### The Breather Sequence

**Also called:** the trough run, recovery block, the quiet stretch
**What it is:** A short, low-pressure sequence placed after a peak, whose job is to let the cost of the peak register and to re-establish what is being fought for.
**Effect on the audience:** It restores their capacity to feel the next peak. Without troughs, escalation stops being escalation and becomes noise.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it directly after a set piece or a major reversal, and roughly once per act. The craft rule: a breather is not a break — it still needs a question, just a small and human one. Can he tell her? Will the boy eat? Will anyone say the dead man's name? The pressure comes down; the drama does not stop. A breather with no question is the scene readers skip, and once they have skipped one they will try skipping the next.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, game narrative | genres: action, war, horror, thriller, fantasy
**Avoid when:** You are in the last act. After the final turn, troughs release tension you cannot rebuild, and the ending goes slack in exactly the place readers judge hardest.
**Example:**
> After the ambush, two scenes:
> 1. They boil water and nobody mentions the third man. Question: will anyone say his name?
> 2. The youngest says it. The sergeant leaves the tent, which is an answer.
> Four minutes, no danger, and the next firefight now costs three times what the last one did.

**Yields to:** `tens.post_climax_hold` — Last act, after the final turn.  
`seq.breather_sequence`

---

### Sequences in Television Acts

**Also called:** the act-as-sequence, broadcast act structure, the break beat
**What it is:** In episodic television, the act is short enough that one act is often one or two sequences, and the act break is the sequence climax plus a dangling cause aimed at the commercial.
**Effect on the audience:** They come back after the break — which in commercial television is the only metric the structure exists to serve.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use this mapping whenever you are writing to a five-act hour or a teaser-plus-four. The craft rule: put the sequence climax at the act break, not before it. The commonest broadcast fault is a run that peaks two minutes early and then walks to the break, so the audience leaves on a lull. If a single act contains two sequences, the first must close with partial resolution and the second's climax is the break. Streaming removes the commercial but not the mechanism — the pause point simply becomes the "still watching" prompt.
**Best in:** formats: hour drama, procedural, soap, half-hour comedy, series, Documentary Series, Heritage / Historical Documentary, Feature Documentary | genres: crime, medical, legal, drama, Documentary, Heritage (civilisation-focused), Educational
**Avoid when:** Writing for a platform with no breaks and a bingeing audience, where every act ending being a cliffhanger flattens into a tic. There, alternate: close one act, hang the next.
**Example:**
> Act Two, one sequence: "Can they get consent to operate?"
> 1. The daughter refuses.
> 2. They look for the estranged son.
> 3. The son agrees — for a reason nobody likes.
> 4. As they scrub in, the daughter arrives with a lawyer. Cut to break.
> The climax and the break are the same beat. That is the whole technique.

`seq.tv_act_sequence`

---

### Sequences in Short-Form Serials

**Also called:** vertical-drama runs, micro-episode sequencing, the two-minute block
**What it is:** In one-to-three-minute serialised episodes, a single sequence is spread across several episodes, so each episode is one or two scenes and the sequence climax lands every third or fourth episode.
**Effect on the audience:** Continuous swipe-through. The episode ends on a scene turn; the sequence ends on a bigger one, and the bigger one is what converts a viewer into a follower.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when writing vertical drama, serialised reels or chapter-a-day fiction apps. The craft rule: every episode needs a turn, but only every third needs a payoff — and you must know which is which before you write, or you will spend all your payoffs in the first week. Keep the sequence question stated aloud on screen, because a viewer arriving mid-run has no earlier context and will leave inside four seconds if they cannot tell what is being fought over.
**Best in:** formats: vertical micro-drama, reels/shorts, web serial, serialised fiction | genres: romance, revenge, thriller, melodrama
**Avoid when:** Adapting long-form material without restructuring. Chopping a feature's sequences into ninety-second slices gives you episodes that end wherever the page break fell, which is the single commonest failure in vertical adaptation.
**Example:**
> Sequence: "Will she prove the contract was forged?" — four episodes.
> Ep 1 (2 min): she finds the signature. Turn: it is her own hand.
> Ep 2: she confronts the secretary. Turn: the secretary is afraid of someone else.
> Ep 3: she gets the original. Turn: the original is a second forgery.
> Ep 4: she shows the board. Sequence climax: they already knew, and the meeting was called to fire her.

**Yields to:** `seq.media_transposition` — Adapting long-form instead of restructuring it.  
`seq.shortform_serial`

---

### The Chapter Cluster

**Also called:** the prose sequence, the movement, the part-within-a-part
**What it is:** The novel's version of the sequence — three to six chapters bound by one question, ending with the chapter that answers it hardest. Usually invisible on the contents page and absolutely present in the reading.
**Effect on the audience:** It produces the "one more chapter" effect, which is really the reader refusing to stop mid-cluster.
**Used for and where it works best:** Use it when outlining any novel over sixty thousand words, and when diagnosing a saggy middle. The craft rule: chapter breaks and cluster breaks must not always coincide. If every cluster ends neatly on a chapter end and every chapter ends on a beat, the book becomes metronomic. Let one cluster end mid-chapter, so the reader turns the page into a new pressure without being told. Mark the clusters in your own manuscript even though the reader will never see a label — this is how you find out that chapters 14 to 19 are asking no question at all.
**Best in:** formats: novel, novella, memoir, serialised fiction, narrative non-fiction | genres: literary fiction, crime, historical, fantasy, thriller
**Avoid when:** Writing a genuinely episodic book — linked stories, a picaresque, a year of diary entries. Clustering those imposes a spine the form has refused on purpose.
**Example:**
> Cluster: chapters 9–13, "Will she stay in the house through the winter?"
> 9. The roof. 10. The neighbour's offer, refused. 11. The first snow and the generator. 12. The neighbour again, and this time he does not ask. 13. She stays — and starts sleeping with the rifle by the bed.
> Five chapters. One question. The answer costs more than leaving would have.

**Yields to:** `seq.short_film_model` — Genuinely episodic book: linked stories, picaresque.  
`seq.chapter_cluster`

---

## Section 5 — Diagnosis and Repair

### Sequence Mapping a Draft

**Also called:** the sequence audit, the one-line-per-run pass, structural x-ray
**What it is:** A diagnostic pass over a finished draft that reduces it to one line per sequence — question, climax, cost — so the mid-level shape becomes visible in a page.
**Effect on the audience:** None. This is the single most useful revision tool in the category, and it is entirely for the writer.
**Used for and where it works best:** Run it on any draft that "sags" without the writer being able to say where. The craft rule for reading the map: look for three specific things. Runs with no question — cut or merge them. Two adjacent runs with the same question — one of them is redundant, and it is usually the first. Runs whose climax is smaller than the run before — reorder or raise. Do this before touching a line of dialogue; polishing a scene that sits inside a sequence you are about to delete is how a month disappears. Compare against `struct.sequence_approach` to see which structural positions are missing rather than merely weak.
**Best in:** formats: feature screenplay, novel, hour drama, series bible | genres: all
**Avoid when:** The draft is not finished. Mapping an incomplete manuscript maps your intentions, which are always better structured than the thing you actually wrote.
**Example:**
> Map of a failing second act:
> Run 4 — Q: can he find the witness? Climax: finds her. Cost: none.
> Run 5 — Q: can he get the witness to talk? Climax: she talks. Cost: none.
> Run 6 — Q: can he get the witness to court? Climax: she comes. Cost: none.
> Three runs, three wins, nothing paid. The diagnosis is not "pacing", it is that nothing in twenty-five minutes cost this man anything, and the fix is to lose two of these three runs and make the survivor expensive.

**Yields to:** `seq.sequence_outline` — Draft not finished; the same document, written ahead.  
`seq.sequence_map`

---

### The Inflated Sequence

**Also called:** the padded run, four scenes of one scene, sequence bloat
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** Material that is genuinely one continuous scene, broken across three or four locations so it will look like a sequence, with each fragment carrying a fraction of a single value turn.
**Effect on the audience:** Tedium disguised as structure. They feel the run taking time without spending any.
**Used for and where it works best:** Recognising it is the technique. The tell: you can state the whole run's content in one sentence with no "and then" in it — "she tells him she is leaving" spread over the kitchen, the car, the office and the pavement. The second tell: you could delete any one of the fragments and lose nothing but minutes. The fix is `scene.merge_two_scenes` applied twice: collapse all four into the hardest location and play the entire turn there, then use the pages you recovered for the run that actually needed to exist.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** —
**Example:**
> Inflated: 1. She starts to tell him in the kitchen; the phone rings. 2. She almost tells him in the car; he changes the radio. 3. She nearly tells him at his office; his colleague comes in. 4. She tells him on the pavement.
> Collapsed: she tells him in the kitchen in the first ninety seconds, and the remaining three scenes are now free to be about what he does with it — which is a sequence, and has a climax.

**Yields to:** `scene.merge_two_scenes` — Collapse the padded run into its hardest location.  
`seq.inflated_sequence`

---

### The Crushed Sequence

**Also called:** the compressed run, the scene doing four scenes' work, the summary beat
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A major movement of the story — a betrayal, an investigation, a conversion — delivered in one scene because the writer was in a hurry, so the audience is told about a change instead of undergoing one.
**Effect on the audience:** Disbelief, located vaguely as "the character wouldn't do that". They did not refuse the event; they refused its speed.
**Used for and where it works best:** Recognising it is the technique. The tells: a scene that requires more than one value turn to work; heavy expository dialogue about offstage events; a decision that reverses a position the character held for forty pages. The fix is to expand it into a real run — the first attempt, the complication, the point of no return, the climax — and to take the pages from an inflated sequence elsewhere in the act, which is almost always available.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** —
**Example:**
> Crushed: "In one scene, the loyal deputy hears the tape, confronts the sheriff, resigns, and joins the other side."
> Expanded to four: he hears the tape and says nothing, and covers for the sheriff out of habit → he tests the sheriff with a small lie and is lied to in return → he goes to the other side to ask a question, not to join, and is given something he cannot give back → he is asked to choose in public, and chooses.
> The event is identical. Only now it is believable, because the reader watched it cost him.

**Yields to:** `seq.sequence_unit` — Expand the summarised movement into a real run.  
`seq.crushed_sequence`

---

### The Climaxless Run

**Also called:** the flat sequence, the run that stops, the sequence with no biggest beat
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A sequence whose scenes are roughly equal in weight, so the run ends because the writer moved on rather than because anything concluded.
**Effect on the audience:** A soft dissolve of attention. They cannot say where they lost interest, because there is no landmark to point at.
**Used for and where it works best:** Recognising it is the technique. The test: rank the scenes in the run by the size of their value turn. If the largest is not last, you have found it. The repairs, in order of preference: reorder so the biggest turn ends the run; raise the last scene's cost until it outweighs the others; or cut the run's tail so the biggest turn becomes the ending. What does not work is adding a new dramatic scene to the end — a climax must arise from the run's own question, and a bolted-on event just makes the run longer and still flat.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** —
**Example:**
> Flat: 1. He learns his brother is in debt (medium). 2. He offers money, refused (medium). 3. He talks to the wife (medium). 4. He decides to wait (small).
> Repaired by reordering and raising: 1. He offers money, refused. 2. He talks to the wife, who tells him not to interfere. 3. He learns the debt is to their father. 4. He pays it in the one currency his brother cannot refuse, and the brother never speaks to him again.
> Same four events. Now the run finishes instead of stopping.

**Yields to:** `seq.sequence_climax` — Reorder so the biggest turn ends the run.  
`seq.climaxless_run`

---

### The Errand Run

**Also called:** the logistics sequence, the getting-there block, plumbing scenes
**This is a named failure, not a recommendation.**
**What it is:** A run of scenes covering the practical movements a plot requires — travel, arrangements, phone calls, arrivals — with no question above scene level, mistaken for a sequence because it occupies the space one would.
**Effect on the audience:** They start reading faster, and they do not slow down again when the real material arrives.
**Used for and where it works best:** Recognising it is the technique. The tell: every scene answers "how did they get here?" and none answers "what will it cost?". The fix is not to delete logistics, it is to make the logistics contested — every errand run can become a real sequence by attaching a deadline, a rival wanting the same thing, or a price. If it cannot take any of those, cut the entire run and open the next sequence with the characters already arrived. Nobody in the history of reading has ever missed a journey that was only a journey.
**Best in:** formats: — | genres: —
**Avoid when:** —
**Example:**
> Errand run: he books the flight; he packs; he says goodbye to the dog; he lands; he takes a taxi; he checks in.
> Fix A, contest it: he books the flight, and the only seat is on the plane his creditor is on.
> Fix B, cut it: "Two days later, in a hotel room in Palermo, he opened the envelope."
> Fix B is right roughly nine times out of ten.

**Yields to:** `seq.journey_sequence` — Contest the logistics; each stage removes a resource.  
`seq.errand_run`
